Board game brings oral health inequalities research to life
resumen_original: Board game brings oral health inequalities research to life A new board game developed by University of Liverpool researchers is creating opportunities for students, health professionals and other stakeholders to explore the social factors that influence oral health and access to dental care. Informed by findings from more than 70 in-depth interviews, the prototype game offers an interactive way to understand the barriers people can face in maintaining their oral health and accessing dental services. It explores how wider social determinants of health, including occupation, poverty, the cost-of-living crisis and global events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, can shape people's experiences. The research informing the game draws on two national projects: a study published in the British Dental Journal exploring the oral health needs of sex workers and a study examining oral health stigma and shame. This wider work has been described as "bold and important" in an editorial in the British Dental Journal. The board game has significant potential as a teaching and training resource across a range of disciplines, including dentistry, criminology, biomedical sciences, public health and planning. By placing players in situations that encourage discussion and reflection, it provides an accessible way to engage with the complex realities behind oral health inequalities. It also offers opportunities to involve health professionals and other key stakeholders in conversations about the challenges people face in maintaining their oral health, accessing dental care and living with dignity and confidence. The game was recently showcased at three Liverpool venues as part of the ESRC Festival of Social Science, giving members of the public an opportunity to try the prototype. It builds on an art exhibition exploring the oral health experiences of sex workers, which is now set to tour U.K. dental schools. The project team, led by clinical lecturer in dentistry Dr. Janine Yazdi-Doughty and senior lecturer in criminology Dr. Gemma Ahearne, is keen to explore its potential for teaching, training and public engagement. Ahearne said, "The game provides an opportunity for students on our largest optional module in my department—Crime, Justice and the Sex Industry—to engage with our research through gamification."

resumen_original: The UK Government must strengthen action on tobacco, alcohol and HPV vaccination as mouth cancer diagnoses in England rise by 40% in a decade, the Oral Health Foundation has warned. Its new report,1 released on 6 November for Mouth Cancer Action Month, calls for funded support to stop using tobacco, minimum unit pricing and cancer warnings on alcohol in England, and catch-up HPV vaccination for young people who have missed out. The charity also demands better access to NHS dentistry so people at higher risk can receive advice and have worrying changes checked promptly. NHS England figures show 9,673 mouth cancer cases were diagnosed in 2024, compared with 6,908 in 2014. Across the UK, 3,650 people died from the disease in 2024 – equivalent to ten deaths a day. ‘Tobacco, Alcohol, HPV: Closing the Risk Factor Gap'1 sets out 11 priorities covering prevention, earlier diagnosis and support after treatment. Dr Rachael England, Head of Policy and Advocacy at the Oral Health Foundation, said: ‘People need practical help to stop using tobacco, stronger alcohol policies and accessible HPV vaccination. They also need timely access to a dentist or doctor when they notice a worrying change in their mouth. ‘If we fail to act, we risk more preventable cancers and more people waiting too long for a diagnosis. The Government must make prevention and early diagnosis a priority, backed by sustained funding and services people can actually access.' The report calls for sustained stop-smoking funding, clear referral routes and stronger tobacco controls. It also recommends support developed with South Asian communities for people using smokeless tobacco. The report also highlights England's failure to update its alcohol strategy since 2012 and calls for a new strategy that tackles cancer risk, introduces minimum unit pricing and sets a timetable for alcohol labels carrying cancer warnings and drinking guidelines. It warns of missed opportunities to prevent HPV-related cancers, with more than a quarter of Year 8 girls and a third of boys in England not vaccinated against HPV in 2024/25. resumen_original: The GBT Summit World Tour London 2026 brought together leading voices from dentistry and wider healthcare for a packed programme that explored how prevention is changing clinical practice, patient care and the business of dentistry. Periodontist Dr Devan Raindi explored minimally invasive non-surgical therapy and the role of biofilm management in periodontal treatment. The programme also considered developments that could influence how practices work in the years ahead. Dentist and practice owner Dr Simon Chard joined Dr Christian Leonhart to discuss artificial intelligence in dentistry, while Celso Da Costa, General Manager of EMS, addressed the business of prevention and how practices can make preventive care an integral part of their clinical and commercial approach. resumen_original: The recent NHS England Digital update confirming that the Reasonable Adjustment Flag is mandatory across publicly funded health and social care services in England, with clinical system suppliers now being onboarded, is welcome.1 We would urge colleagues to recognise that paediatric dentistry is a key setting, and that the flag has the potential to significantly benefit children with additional needs. The Flag is a national record on the NHS Spine showing that a person needs reasonable adjustments and, with consent, what they are. Its categories read like a paediatric dental new patient proforma: anxiety related to clinical settings, needle phobia, noise intolerance, familiarisation visits, extended or first appointments, and distraction for procedures.1 Too often this information reaches us in an incomplete referral letter, or not at all. Families repeat their story at reception, and teams discover needs at the chairside, when they are hardest to meet. The legal duty to make reasonable adjustments is anticipatory,1 and anticipation depends on information arriving before the child does. This complements the shift ‘from analogue to digital' in the NHS 10 Year Health Plan, which commits to a single patient record so patients need not retell their history, and to a digital child health ‘red book'.2 For paediatric dentistry to benefit from this, dental practice and hospital record systems must be able to read and contribute the Flag. Dental teams across commissioning levels need smartcard access and training in the National Care Records Service, and electronic referral pathways should prompt referrers to check and record adjustments. Otherwise, dentistry risks remaining a fragmented, analogue service in a digital NHS. The need is acute in London. Specialist (level 2) and consultant-led (level 3) paediatric services, as defined in national commissioning guidance,3 see a high proportion of children with additional needs, including autism, learning disability, ADHD, sensory processing differences and complex medical conditions. Many require sedation or general anaesthesia. resumen_original: Abstract Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) adapt to the microenvironment by reprogramming their cellular metabolism, leading to diverse immunomodulatory functions and inconsistent outcomes for MSC-based therapies in inflammatory diseases. Glutamine, an immunonutrient, plays key roles in immune regulation and MSC physiology; however, whether glutamine contributes to MSC immunomodulation and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate that glutamine metabolism sustains the immunomodulatory function and therapeutic efficacy of dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs), mediated by metabolite α-ketoglutarate (αKG), using both acute colitis model and acute lung injury model. The glutamine–αKG axis induces the expression of the anti-inflammatory genes TGF-β1, PTGS2, and TSG6, thereby increasing the therapeutic efficacy of DPSCs. Mechanistically, αKG orchestrates an epigenetic switch via two pathways: promoting JMJD3-dependent demethylation of the repressive mark H3K27me3 and simultaneously fueling the TCA cycle to increase citrate and acetyl-CoA levels, thereby facilitating H3K27 acetylation. This coordinated H3K27me3-to-H3K27ac switch synergistically maintains the expression of anti-inflammatory genes and the immunomodulatory function of DPSCs. Furthermore, priming DPSCs with αKG or a methyltransferase inhibitor to promote the H3K27me3-to-H3K27ac switch enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of these cells. Collectively, our study provides the first evidence that the glutamine–αKG axis regulates DPSC immunomodulation via a novel metabolic–epigenetic mechanism, highlighting metabolic regulation and epigenetic reprogramming as promising strategies to potentiate MSC-based therapies. titulo_original: Do generative AI chatbots align with high-level evidence in dentistry? A comparison with Cochrane systematic reviews
resumen_original: Abstract Aims/Objectives Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support clinical decision-making; however, their alignment with high-level evidence remains uncertain. This cross-sectional methodological study evaluated the agreement between responses generated by ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek and Cochrane systematic reviews with meta-analyses in dentistry, and assessed short-term response stability. Methods The study was reported according to the Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool (CHART) guideline. Eligible reviews included meta-analyses reporting dichotomous primary outcomes and objective clinical recommendations enabling a clearly defined direction of effect. Standardized PICO-based prompts were submitted to ChatGPT (GPT-4), Gemini (1.5 Flash), and DeepSeek (R1-V3.2-Exp) at three time points using independent chat sessions. Responses were classified as complete agreement, partial agreement, or complete disagreement with the reference standard, and stability was analyzed descriptively. Results Eleven systematic reviews generated 99 chatbot interactions. Gemini and DeepSeek demonstrated complete short-term response stability (100%), whereas ChatGPT produced consistent responses in 72.7% of scenarios. Complete agreement with the reference standard was observed in 45.5% of clinical scenarios for ChatGPT and Gemini and in 27.3% for DeepSeek, while complete disagreement occurred in 0%, 9.1%, and 27.3% of clinical scenarios, respectively. Main discrepancies involved omission of clinically relevant information, incomplete reporting of evidence certainty, and overestimation of treatment effects. Discussion Although LLMs demonstrated high short-term stability, their agreement with dental evidence varied considerably. ChatGPT showed the lowest frequency of complete disagreement, whereas DeepSeek had the highest. Conclusions These findings indicate that current LLMs may assist evidence retrieval and clinical education but require professional verification before clinical application. resumen_original: The article highlights how preventive dental care supports oral health, early detection, and long-term overall wellness. KERNERSVILLE, N.C., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Why are regular dental hygiene visits important even for people who brush and floss consistently at home? HelloNation answers that question in an article featuring insights from Dental Expert Dr. Jesse A. Grimm of Kernersville, NC. The article explains that maintaining good oral health involves more than daily brushing and flossing. Even patients with strong home care routines may still develop plaque buildup, tartar, gum disease, or tooth decay over time. According to the article, regular dental hygiene visits help prevent these issues while allowing dental professionals to identify concerns early before symptoms become more serious or difficult to treat. One of the most important benefits of regular dental hygiene visits is early detection. Cavities, gum disease, and other oral health concerns often begin quietly without causing immediate discomfort. Many individuals may not realize a problem exists until visible damage or pain develops. Routine dental visits give dentists and hygienists the opportunity to identify small concerns early, when treatment may be simpler and less invasive. The article highlights gum disease as one example of a condition that may progress gradually without obvious symptoms in the early stages. Mild gum inflammation may eventually develop into more serious periodontal disease if left untreated. During regular dental hygiene visits, dental professionals evaluate gum health carefully and look for signs of bleeding, infection, inflammation, or gum recession. Early treatment and preventive care may help reduce the risk of long-term gum damage and tooth loss. Professional dental cleanings are another major focus discussed in the article. While brushing and flossing remain essential for daily oral health, they may not completely remove hardened tartar buildup. Over time, plaque may harden into tartar along the gumline and between teeth, creating areas where bacteria can collect more easily. Professional dental cleanings help remove this buildup while lowering the risk of gum disease and tooth decay. The article also explains that patients attending regular dental hygiene visits often receive more personalized guidance regarding home care habits.

resumen_original: Abstract Introduction Incorporating group work into teaching has been associated with increased academic achievement, comprehension, and student satisfaction with their learning. According to social cognitive theory, self-efficacy also plays a critical personal factor that shapes human behaviour. Self-efficacy also influences individuals’ motivation, learning, and task performance. Therefore practice-orientated interactive group work may build self-efficacy in multiple ways, including students’ beliefs and persistence to complete tasks. By encouraging students to evaluate their own performance and receive feedback from peers can promote deeper engagement with the learning processes. The emphasis on critical reflection and reflective practice provides a sound foundation for achieving desired learning outcomes. However, how best to achieve these learning outcomes, either through individual or collective work performance remains unknown. This study aimed to evaluate the contribution of group learning to the development of reflective writing skills by exploring the association between reflection scores and General Self-Efficacy (GSE) scale in dental undergraduate students. Methods A randomised non-blinded control study was designed to assess dental undergraduate students’ reflective performance. Their reflective writing practices were assessed using a rubric guide. Neil Sikka, director of dentistry at Bupa Dental Care, said dental teams could begin closing that awareness gap during routine appointments. ‘Most people don’t even realise that we do an oral cancer screen as part of our normal check-ups,’ he said. Results Of 641 records, 12 systematic reviews met the eligibility criteria; six incorporated quantitative synthesis/meta-analysis, whereas the remaining reviews used structured qualitative synthesis. Regarding the outcomes assessed, 2 reviews focused on postoperative pain, 7 on clinical/radiographic success, and 3 addressed both. All compared only one VPT technique -full pulpotomy- with NSRCT; no eligible reviews provided outcomes for other VPTs. The evidence ultimately drew on 11 unique primary studies. Across reviews, full pulpotomy often achieved short- to medium-term outcomes comparable to NSRCT. Although eligibility criteria covered other VPT modalities, no eligible randomized evidence comparing partial pulpotomy or direct pulp capping with NSRCT was identified. AI may support structured appraisal, but should augment rather than replace expert judgment. Participants will be analyzed according to their original randomized allocation, irrespective of treatment adherence or discontinuation. resumen_original: Abstract Aim This systematic review aimed to summarize the factors that can influence the success rate of restoration repair. Methods A search was carried out in the PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, Web of Science and ProQuest databases in January 2026. Inclusion criteria were randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) with data on restoration repair; and exclusion criteria were follow-up less than 12 months, loss to follow-up higher than 30%, studies, evaluating anterior teeth and unclear evaluation criteria. The risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2 tool for RCTs and ROBINS-I for NRSIs, and the certainty of evidence with the GRADE tool. A single-arm meta-analysis assessed the pooled proportion (95% CI) of repair success rates. Subgroup meta-analyses were also performed. Results Ten studies were included in the final qualitative and quantitative synthesis; however, only seven studies (five RCTs and two NRSIs) were eligible for meta-analysis after stratification by follow-up time. The studies included 302 participants and 542 repaired restorations. The most consistently reported follow-up periods for quantitative analysis were 24 and 120 months. The estimated overall success rates ranged from 78% (95% CI: 67 to 88) in RCTs to 82% (95% CI: 57 to 100) in NRSIs. Discussion No factors were identified as significantly influencing repair success, likely reflecting the limited number of studies and the substantial heterogeneity of the available evidence. Most RCTs presented some concerns regarding risk of bias, especially related to study registration and deviations from intended interventions. Among NRSIs, risk of bias varied from low to moderate due to missing data. Only studies involving permanent teeth were eligible. Interpretation of these findings is limited by the low to very low certainty of the evidence, the small number of eligible studies, substantial methodological heterogeneity, and imprecision of the pooled estimates. Conclusion Although the available evidence suggests favourable long-term outcomes for retoration repair in permanent teeth, the low to very-low certainty of evidence and substancial heterogeneity limit confidence in these findings. Further well-designed studies are needed to clarify the determinants of repair outcomes and strengthen evidence-based clinical decision-making. Access options Subscribe to this journal

resumen_original: A study published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases with Biotia, Bumrungrad International Hospital, and Chulalongkorn University finds that pathogen identification combined with resistance interpretation is what could turn the result into a treatment decision. NEW YORK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A metagenomic sequencing report could have changed the antibiotic decision in 4 out of 10 initial prescriptions for urinary tract infections (UTIs), according to a peer-reviewed study published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases. The report could have flagged antibiotics likely to fail and identified patients who could step down from broad-spectrum drugs. The study was a collaboration between Bumrungrad International Hospital, Chulalongkorn University, and Biotia. It evaluated Biotia's bioinformatics software, BIOTIA-DX, on sequencing data from urine samples collected at a tertiary hospital in Bangkok, Thailand – a setting where antibiotic resistance in uropathogens is high. "Antimicrobial resistance is one of the defining health challenges of our time, and every antibiotic decision matters. This study moves the conversation beyond whether sequencing can find a pathogen to whether it can help doctors choose the right treatment sooner. We're proud to have done this work with our partners at Bumrungrad and Chulalongkorn", said Niamh O'Hara, PhD, the CEO and Co-Founder of Biotia. UTIs are among the most common reasons antibiotics are prescribed. Because standard culture results are often followed by susceptibility testing, the results can take several days to return, requiring doctors to start treatment without knowing the pathogen or its resistance profile. That gap puts patients at risk of ineffective treatment and fuels the spread of drug resistance, and the possibility of infections that have no treatment options. In this study, researchers compared BIOTIA-DX results with standard culture and susceptibility testing in 251 urine samples collected from symptomatic patients. They then examined 54 antibiotic prescriptions written on the day each sample was collected, to ask whether a same-day metagenomic report would have changed the clinical treatment decision. Au-delà de ces indicateurs économiques, l’UNAPL rappelle le rôle quotidien joué par ces professionnels auprès de la population. titulo_original: Implants dentaires : quarante ans après leur pose, des patients toujours satisfaits
resumen_original: Près de quarante ans après la mise en place de leurs implants, les patients demeurent extrêmement satisfaits de leur fonction, malgré une appréciation plus contrastée de leur rendu esthétique. C’est la principale conclusion d’une étude suédoise publiée le 21 octobre dernier dans Clinical Implant Dentistry and Related Research , qui offre l’un des reculs les plus longs jamais rapportés sur des traitements implantaires. Ces résultats revêtent une portée particulière. Les patients étudiés ont été traités entre 1982 et 1985 à l’Université de Göteborg, berceau des travaux du professeur Per-Ingvar Brånemark, dont les recherches sur l’ostéointégration ont jeté les bases de l’implantologie moderne. Cette situation unique permet aujourd’hui aux chercheurs de documenter le devenir clinique et le ressenti des patients près de quatre décennies après la pose des implants. L’étude fait suite à des travaux publiés en 2025 montrant que les 18 implants retrouvés chez ces patients étaient toujours en fonction après près de 40 ans. Les chercheurs ont cette fois cherché à évaluer le point de vue des patients eux-mêmes. Treize d’entre eux ont répondu à des questionnaires portant sur leur satisfaction globale, la fonction masticatoire, l’esthétique des restaurations et leur qualité de vie liée à la santé orale. Les résultats sont particulièrement favorables sur le plan fonctionnel. Sur une échelle de 0 à 100, les patients ont attribué une note moyenne de 93 au résultat global du traitement et de 96 à sa fonction malgré le temps écoulé. Les patients notent également un impact limité de leur état bucco-dentaire sur leur qualité de vie quotidienne. Des écarts esthétiques mais un très haut niveau de satisfaction Ces données apportent un éclairage complémentaire aux habituels critères de succès implantaire. Au-delà des taux de survie, une restauration peut conserver une très forte valeur d’usage pour le patient plusieurs décennies après sa mise en fonction. L’analyse esthétique apparaît en revanche plus nuancée.
